slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: g/L, g/dL

What it is used for: A hemoglobin test is most often used to check for anemia, a condition in which the body does not make enough healthy red blood cells. Hemoglobin is usually measured as part of a complete blood count (CBC).

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: The test may be part of a routine exam or ordered for symptoms of anemia (weakness, dizziness, cold hands and feet); a family history of thalassemia, sickle cell anemia or another inherited blood disorder; a diet low in iron and other minerals; a long-term infection; or heavy blood loss from an injury or surgery. It is also used to monitor treatment of anemia and other conditions that affect hemoglobin.

Physiology: Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein in red blood cells. It carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body; cells need oxygen to grow, reproduce and make energy. Hemoglobin levels give information about the health of red blood cells.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: High hemoglobin may be a sign of lung disease, heart disease, polycythemia vera (the bone marrow makes too many red blood cells) or sleep apnea (breathing repeatedly stops during sleep). Living at a higher altitude can also raise hemoglobin.

Low hemoglobin may be a sign of different types of anemia, thalassemia, iron deficiency, liver disease, cancer and other diseases, blood loss from injury, a heavy menstrual period or other problems, or a lack of nutrients such as iron or vitamin B12.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: WHO (2024) also grades anemia severity by hemoglobin. In adults aged 15–65, mild anemia is 110–119 g/L in non-pregnant women and 110–129 g/L in men; moderate is 80–109 g/L; severe is below 80 g/L. In all trimesters of pregnancy, severe anemia is below 70 g/L.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/9
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a hemoglobin test. If other tests are ordered on the same sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/9
bullets: WHO recommends measuring hemoglobin in venous blood on automated hematology analyzers with high-quality control measures. Capillary and venous results clearly differ, but the size of the difference has not been confirmed, so no adjustment is given to make capillary results comparable with venous ones.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/9
bullets: Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/9
bullets: Interferences: Diet, activity level, certain medicines, dehydration, smoking and certain genetic conditions can affect the result.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/9
bullets: WHO recommends adjusting for the elevation of residence above sea level and for smoking when diagnosing anemia: the adjustment is subtracted from the observed hemoglobin or added to the anemia cutoff. For example, the adjustment is 8 g/L for 1000–1499 m and 5 g/L for smoking 10–19 cigarettes a day.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 6/9
bullets: On analysers haemoglobin can be falsely high with lipaemia, marked leukocytosis or paraproteinaemia, which make the lysate turbid. If haemoglobin does not fit the RBC and MCV, the result is checked.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 7/9
bullets: Limitations: The test cannot tell what causes an abnormal level, but how high or low it is helps judge severity. The reference range varies with the laboratory, age, race and sex; results are interpreted with symptoms, history and other blood tests.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 8/9
bullets: The WHO cutoffs are based on the 5th percentile of healthy people: about 5% of healthy individuals have hemoglobin below the cutoff and may be falsely diagnosed as anemic.
A hemoglobin test is not the same as a hemoglobin A1C test, which checks average blood glucose.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 9/9
bullets: The Sahli (acid haematin, visual comparison) method is obsolete: the WHO manual calls the haemiglobincyanide photometric method the most accurate and recommends it wherever possible. Aripova et al. (2007) also note that Sahli is not standardised.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: Hematocrit is often part of a complete blood count. It is used to check general health and to help diagnose or monitor blood disorders such as anemia (too few red blood cells) and polycythemia (erythrocytosis, an uncommon disorder with too many red blood cells and blood that becomes too thick).

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: The test may be part of a routine checkup, monitoring during cancer treatment or an ongoing condition, or ordered for symptoms of anemia (shortness of breath, weakness, headache, dizziness, arrhythmia) or of polycythemia (headache, shortness of breath when lying down, itching after a shower, a red face, heavy sweating especially during sleep, blurred vision, unusual bleeding from the gums or nose).

Physiology: Hematocrit measures what percent of the blood is made up of red blood cells. The rest is white blood cells, platelets and a liquid called plasma. For example, a result of 42 means 42% of the blood is red blood cells.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: A high hematocrit may come from making too many red blood cells (lung disease, congenital heart disease, heart failure, polycythemia) or from low blood plasma due to dehydration (the most common cause of a high hematocrit) or shock. Living at a high altitude also raises it, because the body makes more red cells when oxygen is low.

A low hematocrit may be a sign of recent blood loss from an injury, chronic blood loss, anemia or the body making too many white blood cells (bone marrow disease, leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma or cancer that has spread to the bone marrow). Pregnancy can lower the hematocrit because the body holds more fluid.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Interferences: On analysers haematocrit is often not measured directly — it approximates the product of the red cell count and MCV. So an error in RBC or MCV (e.g., cold agglutinins, hyperglycaemia, prolonged storage) carries over to the haematocrit.

Limitations: Normal hematocrit varies with sex, age, smoking and the altitude where one lives — compare with the interval on the lab report and discuss with the provider. A result outside the range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: ×10¹²/L, ×10⁶/µL
What it is used for: An RBC count is almost always part of a complete blood count and helps diagnose red blood cell disorders such as anemia.

An RBC count that is higher or lower than normal is often the first sign of an illness and may allow treatment before symptoms appear. The test is used during treatment that can affect blood counts (such as chemotherapy), to monitor conditions such as chronic kidney disease, and for symptoms of a low count (shortness of breath, weakness, headache, dizziness, arrhythmia, pale skin) or a high count (headache, dizziness, vision problems).

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Red blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the spongy tissue inside large bones. They contain hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to every cell.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Causes of a high RBC count include dehydration, heart disease, polycythemia vera, scarring of the lungs (often from smoking), lung disease, kidney cancer and sleep apnea. Misuse of performance drugs such as anabolic steroids and living at a high altitude can also raise it.

Causes of a low RBC count include anemia, leukemia, malnutrition (not enough calories, vitamins and/or minerals), multiple myeloma, kidney failure, blood loss from injury or other problems, alcohol use disorder and pregnancy.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

Interferences: Diet, activity level, medicines, having a menstrual period, not drinking enough water and other factors can affect CBC results; an abnormal level does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Analyser errors: RBC can be falsely high with marked leukocytosis or hyperlipidaemia and falsely low with cold agglutinins or in-tube haemolysis. In cold agglutination red cells are counted as clumps — RBC is low while MCV and MCHC are falsely high. Dolgov et al. advise warming such a sample to 37 °C and re-measuring. If the result does not fit the clinical picture — flags, smear and repeat.
Limitations: A complete blood count is only one tool: for a diagnosis the provider considers medical history, symptoms and other factors, and more tests may be needed.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: If the count is low or high, more tests may be needed: a reticulocyte count (checks whether the bone marrow makes enough red cells), iron tests and B vitamin tests.
NHLBI notes that some normal ranges differ between men and women, and that age, high altitude and race may also affect them — so the result is compared with the range on the lab report.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: ×10⁹/L, /µL

What it is used for: The test helps diagnose or monitor disorders with a high or low WBC: signs of infection (fever, chills, body aches, headache, a wound that is red, has pus or won’t heal, an ongoing cough), inflammation or autoimmune disease; and a disease or medicine that weakens the immune system — if the count gets too low, the provider may adjust treatment. Children may be tested as part of routine screening.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: White blood cells (leukocytes) are part of the immune system: made in the bone marrow and found in the blood and lymph tissue, they travel through the bloodstream and tissues to where they are needed to fight infections and other diseases. There are five major types — neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils; the WBC measures their total number.

When you get sick, the body makes more white cells to fight bacteria, viruses or other foreign substances, raising the count. Some cancers, HIV (a virus that attacks white cells) and certain medicines such as chemotherapy lower it.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Causes of leukocytosis (a high WBC) include infection, an inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, allergy, leukemia or Hodgkin disease, and tissue damage from a burn or surgery. Smoking, stress, a reaction to a medicine or pregnancy can also raise the count.

Causes of leukopenia (a low WBC) include bone marrow damage from infection, disease or treatments such as chemotherapy, cancers that affect the bone marrow, an autoimmune disorder such as lupus, and HIV.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, but some medicines may need to be stopped before the test, so tell the provider about everything you take. Do not stop any medicine unless the provider says so.
Adults give a sample from a vein. Newborns and young babies have a heel stick; older babies and children give blood from the fingertip or arm.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Interferences: Diet, activity level, medicines, having a menstrual period, not drinking enough water and other factors can affect CBC results; an abnormal level does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

Limitations: A WBC shows whether white cells are too high or too low but cannot confirm a diagnosis; it is usually done with a complete blood count, blood differential, blood smear and/or bone marrow test. The differential shows the amount of each type.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: /µL, ×10⁹/L
What it is used for: A platelet count, often part of a complete blood count, is used to diagnose or monitor conditions that cause too much bleeding or clotting.

Signs of low platelets: bleeding for a long time after a minor cut, nosebleeds, unexplained bruising, pinpoint red spots (petechiae) or purple, red or brown spots (purpura), heavy or long periods, blood in urine or stool. Signs of high platelets: numbness of hands and feet, headache, dizziness, weakness, pain, swelling and warmth in the lower legs.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Platelet function tests check the platelets’ ability to form clots: closure time, viscoelastometry, aggregometry, lumiaggregometry, flow cytometry (only at certain centers) and bleeding time, which was once common but is not used much anymore. They are used in complex surgery, with a personal or family bleeding history, and in people taking blood thinners.

Physiology: Platelets are small blood cells formed in the bone marrow and are essential for blood clotting. When you get hurt, platelets, proteins and cells stick together into a clot that stops the bleeding.
The spleen normally stores about one-third of the body’s platelets; an enlarged spleen may remove or store too many.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/3
bullets: High: Thrombocytosis (a high count) can make blood clot more than needed, and clots can block blood flow. Causes include certain cancers such as lung or breast cancer, anemia, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis), rheumatoid arthritis, a viral or bacterial infection and severe blood loss.

High: A high platelet count not caused by another condition is thrombocythemia (primary or essential); one caused by another disease or condition is thrombocytosis (secondary or reactive), which is more common.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/3
bullets: Low: Thrombocytopenia (a low count) can cause too much bleeding after an injury. Causes include blood cancers such as leukemia or lymphoma; viral infections such as mononucleosis, hepatitis or measles; autoimmune disease; bone marrow infection or damage; cirrhosis; and vitamin B12 deficiency. Mild gestational thrombocytopenia can occur in pregnancy; it is not known to harm mother or fetus and usually resolves on its own.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 3/3
bullets: Low: Heparin, a medicine used to prevent clots, can through an immune reaction cause both clots and thrombocytopenia (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia). Toxic chemicals such as pesticides, arsenic and benzene, and alcohol, can damage the bone marrow and lower platelet production; some medicines can too.

Low: NHLBI defines a low platelet count as less than 150,000/µL: 100,000–150,000/µL is mild and less than 20,000/µL severe; a high count is more than 450,000/µL. The full classification is in the “Decision limits” block.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a platelet count. Before a platelet function test, medicines such as aspirin and ibuprofen may need to be stopped — only as the provider instructs.

With skin punctures the hematology specimen is collected first to minimize the effects of platelet clumping; the venepuncture order is the reverse. If more than two specimens are needed, venepuncture may give more accurate results.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

Limitations: Platelet tests are often done with an MPV (platelet size), PTT and PT/INR. In people taking anti-platelet medicine such as aspirin, platelet function results show how well the medicine is working.
Mild thrombocytopenia often has no symptoms and is often found on a routine blood test.

slides.title: Platelets (PLT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: A complete blood count is only one tool: for a diagnosis the provider considers medical history, symptoms and other factors, and more tests may be needed.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: fL

What it is used for: MCV is usually part of a complete blood count. Because each type of anemia affects red cell size, shape and quality differently, MCV helps identify the type of anemia together with other tests.
Physiology: MCV measures the average size of red blood cells. Cells that are too small or too large may be a sign of anemia, a lack of certain vitamins or other conditions.
NHLBI reports MCV in femtoliters (fL); a femtoliter is a measure of volume.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Larger-than-normal red cells may be a sign of pernicious anemia (from a lack of vitamin B12 or a disease that affects its use, such as certain autoimmune diseases, celiac disease or Crohn’s disease), anemia from a lack of folic acid, or liver disease.

Red cells that are smaller than normal may be a sign of certain anemias, including iron deficiency anemia (the most common form), or of thalassemia (a group of inherited disorders with fewer healthy red cells and less hemoglobin, which can cause severe anemia).

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Interferences: Age, diet, activity level, medicines, menstrual period and other conditions can affect MCV; an abnormal value does not always need treatment.

MCV can be falsely high with cold agglutinins, hyperglycaemia and prolonged sample storage (red cells swell; Dolgov et al. cite storage longer than 8 hours). Severe hyponatraemia can falsely lower it. A sudden change that does not fit previous results suggests an error.
Limitations: MCV alone cannot diagnose a disease. Anemia can occur with a normal MCV — for example, after sudden blood loss, in kidney failure or in aplastic anemia.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Read MCV together with RDW: low MCV with normal RDW — uniform microcytosis (thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease); low MCV with high RDW — iron deficiency likely (check ferritin and transferrin saturation); normal MCV with high RDW — mixed populations (early iron deficiency, combined iron + B12/folate deficiency, after transfusion). The reticulocyte count separates poor production from loss or destruction.

slides.title: Which parameter, which cause
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Analyser spurious results
bullets: RBC: ↑ marked leukocytosis, hyperlipidaemia; ↓ cold agglutinins, haemolysis
Haemoglobin: ↑ lipaemia, marked leukocytosis, paraproteinaemia
MCV: ↑ cold agglutinins, hyperglycaemia, prolonged storage; ↓ severe hyponatraemia
MCHC: ↑ falsely high Hb or falsely low RBC; ↓ hyperglycaemia, prolonged storage
Haematocrit: Calculated from RBC × MCV — their errors carry over
Reticulocytes: ↑ nucleated red cells, inclusions, fluorescent interference

slides.title: MCHC as an error flag
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Analyser spurious results
bullets: MCHC varies little physiologically. Above 36 g/dL (360 g/L) suggests artefact (Takami 2026); Dolgov et al. give 37–38 g/dL.
A truly high MCHC occurs in spherocytosis — check the smear.

slides.title: What to do
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Analyser spurious results · 1/2
bullets: Review analyser flags, inspect the sample (clot, haemolysis, lipaemia), look at the smear and repeat if needed.
If cold agglutination is suspected: warm the sample to 37 °C and re-measure (Dolgov et al.).

slides.title: What to do
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Analyser spurious results · 2/2
bullets: Do not store samples long: Dolgov et al. note MCV rising after more than 8 hours.

slides.title: Example: Counting chamber
slides.eyebrow: Example
bullets: Formula: Cells/µL = cells counted × dilution ÷ (squares counted × area of one square, mm² × chamber depth, mm)
slides.ex: 1 µL = 1 mm³; ×10⁹/L = cells/µL ÷ 1000. WHO example: improved Neubauer, 4 corner squares (1 mm² each), depth 0.1 mm, 1 in 20 dilution, 188 leukocytes → 9.4 × 10⁹/L.

slides.title: According to WHO (2024), below which hemoglobin level is a non-pregnant woman aged 15–65 considered anemic?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the cutoff for non-pregnant women aged 15–65 is 120 g/L (12.0 g/dL).

Basis: WHO Table 2: non-pregnant women < 120 g/L (12.0 g/dL), men < 130 g/L (13.0 g/dL), first and third trimesters < 110 g/L (11.0 g/dL).

slides.title: A patient lives 1,200 m above sea level. What does WHO recommend when assessing anemia?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: An adjustment — 8 g/L (0.8 g/dL) — is added to the cutoff
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: or it is subtracted from the observed value — same result.

Basis: The altitude adjustment — 8 g/L (0.8 g/dL) for 1000–1499 m — is subtracted from observed hemoglobin or added to the anemia cutoff.

slides.title: A hematocrit result is 0.42 L/L (42%). What does it mean?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: 42% of the blood is red cells
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the rest is white cells, platelets and plasma.

Basis: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood made up of red blood cells.

slides.title: According to the source, what is the most common cause of a high hematocrit?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source calls it the most common cause.

Basis: Low plasma — mainly dehydration — raises the hematocrit.

slides.title: Which factor, per the source, can RAISE the red blood cell count?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: less oxygen leads to more red cells.

Basis: High altitude and anabolic steroid misuse raise the count; pregnancy and kidney failure lower it.

slides.title: The RBC count is low. Which follow-up tests does the source list?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Only a repeat complete blood count
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: these are the tests the source lists.

Basis: Reticulocytes check marrow output; iron and B vitamins are needed to make red cells.

slides.title: Methods of counting erythrocytes. Erythrocyte indices?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/3
bullets: 1. Methods of counting erythrocytes: manual – counting cells in a defined volume of diluted blood in a counting chamber (Goryaev/Neubauer); automated – on a hematology analyzer by impedance (Coulter) or optical method. Today's standard is the analyzer; the chamber is only a backup/training method.

2. Sources of error of the chamber method: incorrect dilution, pipette error, incorrect filling of the chamber, double counting of cells on the border (only cells on the upper and left lines are counted), statistical uncertainty due to the small number of cells counted.

slides.title: Methods of counting erythrocytes. Erythrocyte indices?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/3
bullets: 3. Hemoglobin – the reference method is hemiglobincyanide (ICSH); analyzers use cyanide-free photometric variants; hematocrit and indices are derived from values measured/calculated by the analyzer.
4. Erythrocyte indices: MCV = Ht/RBC (80–100 fL), MCH = Hb/RBC (27–32 pg), MCHC = Hb/Ht (hemoglobin concentration), RDW – distribution width by volume (anisocytosis; ~11.5–15%).

slides.title: Methods of counting erythrocytes. Erythrocyte indices?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 3/3
bullets: 5. Classification of anemias by indices: MCV <80 – microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic, chronic disease), 80–100 – normocytic, >100 – macrocytic (megaloblastic: B12/folate; non-megaloblastic: liver, alcohol). MCV + RDW together narrow the differential diagnosis.
6. False results: agglutination of erythrocytes lowers RBC and raises MCV; lipemia falsely raises Hb and MCHC – in such cases examining the smear is mandatory.

slides.title: Erythrocyte indices?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Erythrocyte indices are values derived from RBC, Hb and Ht that show erythrocyte volume and hemoglobin content; they are used in determining the cause of anemia and in internal laboratory quality control.
2. MCV (mean volume) = Ht/RBC; normal 80–100 fL: microcytosis (<80), normocytosis, macrocytosis (>100).

3. MCH (mean amount of Hb in one erythrocyte) = Hb/RBC, ~27–32 pg; MCHC (Hb concentration in the erythrocyte) = Hb/Ht: decrease – hypochromia; increase – spherocytosis, xerocytosis or artifact (lipemia, agglutination).

slides.title: Erythrocyte indices?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. RDW – SD or CV (%) of the MCV distribution curve, a measure of anisocytosis; ~11.5–15%. For example, in iron deficiency RDW is usually increased, which helps to distinguish it from thalassemia trait.
5. Clinical use: separate the type of anemia by MCV, then choose tests such as iron parameters, reticulocytes, B12/folate.
6. Each laboratory uses its own reference intervals; abnormal indices are confirmed with a peripheral blood smear.

slides.title: Factors affecting the erythrocyte sedimentation rate?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/3
bullets: 1. ESR is the sedimentation of erythrocytes in citrated blood over 1 hour (mm/h); a nonspecific marker of inflammation, depending mainly on the formation of "rouleaux" (stacks of coins) by erythrocytes under the influence of fibrinogen and immunoglobulins.

2. Reference method – Westergren (ICSH gold standard since 1973): a tube with an internal diameter of 2.5 mm and length of 190–300 mm, 3.2% sodium citrate, and the height of the plasma column is measured after 1 hour in a vertical position. ICSH 2017 gives validation requirements for alternative automated methods.

slides.title: Factors affecting the erythrocyte sedimentation rate?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/3
bullets: 3. Factors increasing ESR: fibrinogen and immunoglobulins (acute phase, myeloma), anemia, female sex, pregnancy, old age; technical: high room temperature, tube tilted by 3° (ESR rises by up to ~30%), air bubbles, sunlight, vibration.
4. Decreasing factors: polycythemia (viscosity), sickle cells, spherocytosis (no rouleaux formation), delaying the sample for more than 2 hours, clotted blood; some drugs (statins, NSAIDs).

slides.title: Factors affecting the erythrocyte sedimentation rate?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 3/3
bullets: 5. Reference values depend on age and sex (for example, under 50 years men ≤15, women ≤20 mm/h; after 50, ≤20 and ≤30 respectively) – the laboratory establishes its own interval.
6. Clinical significance: nonspecific; important in giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myeloma; in acute inflammation CRP changes faster.
